entries.title: Focus on what you can influence
entries.quote: Some things are in our control and others not.
entries.attribution: Epictetus, Enchiridion §1, translated by Elizabeth Carter
entries.summary: Epictetus separates our choices from outcomes shaped by other people and circumstances. Before an important conversation, you can prepare carefully, speak honestly, and listen well, but you cannot guarantee agreement. The distinction can help direct effort toward what you can influence while making room for disappointment without treating it as proof that you acted badly or should stop trying.
entries.question: Where are you judging your effort by an outcome you cannot guarantee?

entries.title: Interrupting retaliation
entries.quote: Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world.
entries.attribution: The Buddha, Dhammapada 5, translated by Acharya Buddharakkhita
entries.summary: This Buddhist teaching asks us to interrupt the impulse to answer hostility with more hostility. In an argument, a reply designed to humiliate someone may satisfy the urge to retaliate while keeping the conflict alive; a firm response that addresses the behavior can serve a different purpose. Read as an ethical discipline, the verse invites you to resist cruelty without requiring reconciliation, continued contact, or acceptance of mistreatment.
entries.question: What would a firm response look like if hurting back were not the goal?

entries.title: Time alone does not bring progress
entries.quote: Actually, time itself is neutral; it can be used either destructively or constructively.
entries.attribution: Martin Luther King Jr., “Letter from Birmingham Jail,” in Why We Can’t Wait
entries.summary: King challenges the belief that racial injustice will disappear if people simply wait long enough: progress requires deliberate effort, while delay can protect an unfair system. His argument also offers a useful test of leadership in everyday settings, where postponing an uncomfortable conversation can leave someone else carrying the cost. Patience has value when it supports a concrete plan; without one, it can become an excuse for avoiding responsibility.
entries.question: Who bears the cost of a problem you are waiting to address?

sources.title: King Institute: Letter from Birmingham Jail

entries.title: Question the values you inherit
entries.quote: we must first question the very value of these values
entries.attribution: Friedrich Nietzsche, On the Genealogy of Morals, Preface §6, translated by Ian Johnston
entries.summary: Nietzsche proposes examining where our moral ideals came from and what kinds of lives they encourage. Applied to everyday life, this invites you to examine whether calling constant self-sacrifice admirable helps people flourish or makes it harder to set reasonable boundaries. An ideal’s origins do not automatically disprove it, but investigating its effects can help you decide whether it deserves your loyalty.
entries.question: Which expectation do you treat as a moral duty without knowing why?

sources.title: On the Genealogy of Morals — Preface §6

entries.title: Attention shapes experience
entries.quote: My experience is what I agree to attend to.
entries.attribution: William James, The Principles of Psychology, Chapter XI (1890)
entries.summary: James argues that attention shapes which parts of the world become vivid and meaningful to us. During a conversation, rehearsing your reply can leave you with a different experience from listening closely to what the other person is trying to say. His nineteenth-century account offers a useful lens on daily life, though its language of choice should not imply that every distraction or distressing thought is under voluntary control.
entries.question: What deserves more of your attention than it currently receives?

sources.title: The Principles of Psychology — Chapter XI: Attention

entries.title: When learning reveals injustice
entries.quote: It had given me a view of my wretched condition, without the remedy.
entries.attribution: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter VII
entries.summary: Douglass reflects that learning to read helped him recognize slavery’s injustice, while knowledge alone could not free him. Understanding a problem can bring discomfort before it brings a way to act; that discomfort does not make the knowledge worthless.
entries.question: What have you learned that made you less comfortable but more aware?

sources.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapter VII

entries.title: Understand the strongest objection
entries.quote: He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.
entries.attribution: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter II
entries.summary: Mill argues that understanding a belief requires hearing its strongest objections from people who actually hold them. In a disagreement with a friend or teammate, explaining their reasoning fairly can reveal a concern that your own argument overlooks. This does not require treating every position as equally credible; it means giving your confidence something harder to answer than a weak version of the opposing view.
entries.question: Could someone who disagrees with you recognize their position in your explanation of it?

entries.title: What we practice, we become
entries.quote: States of character arise out of like activities.
entries.attribution: Aristotle · Nicomachean Ethics, II.1 · W. D. Ross translation
entries.summary: Aristotle connects character to repeated choices. Patience, honesty, and courage take shape through practice, not just good intentions.
entries.question: What quality do your everyday habits give you the most practice in?
